title: Veterans Day 1955: The Men Who Came Home and Built America

scenes.text: It's November eleventh, nineteen fifty-five. A cold, bright morning in a small American town. The high school band is warming up at the end of Main Street. Flags hang from every lamppost. And along the sidewalk, families are waiting, bundled in coats, to watch the men march by. Men in their thirties, a little heavier now, wearing old uniforms that don't quite fit anymore. The veterans.
scenes.query: 1950s Veterans Day parade small town flags
scenes.caption: NOVEMBER 11, 1955

scenes.text: Just a year earlier, in nineteen fifty-four, Congress had changed the name of the holiday. For decades, November eleventh had been Armistice Day, honoring the end of the First World War. Now it was Veterans Day, to honor all American veterans, including the more than sixteen million who had served in the Second World War, and the millions more who had just come home from Korea.
scenes.caption: FROM ARMISTICE DAY TO VETERANS DAY

scenes.text: So today, let's remember them. The men, and women, who came home from war and built the America many of us grew up in. Where they had been, what they came home to, and what they did next. If your father or grandfather was one of them, this one is for him.
scenes.caption: THIS ONE IS FOR HIM

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-five, most of the men in that parade had been in uniform just ten or twelve years before. They had been eighteen, nineteen, twenty years old. Farm boys who had never been more than fifty miles from home. City kids from the factories. Young men from every state and every background.
scenes.caption: EIGHTEEN, NINETEEN, TWENTY

scenes.text: They had trained in places they'd never heard of, then shipped out to North Africa, Italy, France, Germany, and islands across the Pacific. They had flown bombers over Europe, served on ships in the Atlantic, and landed on beaches in Normandy, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. More than four hundred thousand Americans did not come home.
scenes.caption: MORE THAN 400,000 DID NOT COME HOME

scenes.text: And they were not only men. About three hundred and fifty thousand American women served in uniform during the Second World War, as nurses, pilots ferrying planes, clerks, mechanics and radio operators. Millions more worked in the factories at home. By nineteen fifty-five, many of those women were mothers, and some marched in the parade too.
scenes.caption: 350,000 WOMEN SERVED

scenes.text: Back home, everyone had done their part. Families planted victory gardens, bought war bonds, saved scrap metal and lived with rationing of sugar, meat, gasoline and tires. Mothers hung a little flag with a blue star in the front window for every son in uniform. Children collected tin cans and newspapers. The whole country was in it together.
scenes.caption: THE WHOLE COUNTRY WAS IN IT

scenes.text: When the war ended in nineteen forty-five, millions of servicemen came home almost at once. Troop ships sailed into New York, Boston and San Francisco. Trains carried men across the country. Families waited at the station, holding signs. Wives and mothers who hadn't seen their men in three or four years ran down the platform.
scenes.query: 1940s soldiers returning home train station family
scenes.caption: THE HOMECOMING

scenes.text: Many of those men had changed. They had seen things they would never talk about. Some came home with wounds, some with nightmares. In those days, people called it battle fatigue, and most men were simply expected to put it behind them and get on with life. Most of them did, quietly, for the rest of their lives.
scenes.caption: THEY NEVER TALKED ABOUT IT

scenes.text: Many had married quickly before shipping out, and now came home to wives they barely knew, and sometimes children they had never met. A three-year-old might hide behind his mother's skirt when a stranger in uniform walked through the door. It took time for those families to become families again, and most of them did.
scenes.caption: A CHILD HE HAD NEVER MET

scenes.text: And they came home in a hurry to get started. They had lost years. They wanted jobs, wives, houses and children, and they wanted them now. In nineteen forty-six, a record number of Americans got married. And then, starting that same year, came the babies. The baby boom had begun.
scenes.caption: IN A HURRY

scenes.text: The country had made them a promise. In June of nineteen forty-four, even before the war ended, President Roosevelt signed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act. Everyone called it the G.I. Bill. It offered veterans money for college or job training, low-interest home loans, and help while they looked for work.
scenes.caption: THE G.I. BILL

scenes.text: The results were astonishing. By nineteen fifty-six, about seven point eight million World War Two veterans had used the G.I. Bill for education or training. More than two million went to college. In nineteen forty-seven, veterans made up nearly half of all college students in America. Campuses were so crowded that students lived in Quonset huts and trailers.
scenes.caption: HALF OF ALL COLLEGE STUDENTS

scenes.text: Many of those men were the first in their families ever to go to college. Sons of coal miners became engineers. Sons of farmers became doctors. Sons of immigrants became lawyers, teachers and scientists. The G.I. Bill created a huge new American middle class in a single generation.
scenes.caption: THE FIRST IN THEIR FAMILIES

scenes.text: Not every veteran shared equally in those benefits. Black veterans, especially in the South, often found that banks would not give them G.I. Bill home loans, and that many colleges would not admit them. Many of those men came home determined to change that. Their service, and their frustration, helped fuel the civil rights movement of the fifties and sixties.
scenes.caption: NOT EVERYONE SHARED EQUALLY

scenes.text: The G.I. Bill also backed millions of home loans, often with no money down. That's how many of the new suburbs got built. Places like Levittown were full of veterans and their young families. By nineteen fifty-five, a man who had been sleeping in a foxhole ten years earlier might be mowing his own lawn on a Saturday morning.
scenes.caption: FROM FOXHOLE TO FRONT LAWN

scenes.text: And then they went to work, and they built. In nineteen fifty-five, the veterans of the Second World War were in their thirties, at the peak of their strength. They worked in the steel mills, the auto plants and the oil fields. They built highways, bridges, dams, schools, hospitals and whole new towns.
scenes.caption: THEY BUILT

scenes.text: The skills they'd learned in the war came home with them. Men who had repaired airplanes became mechanics. Radio operators became electricians and engineers. Navy cooks opened diners. Army engineers built roads. Pilots flew for the new airlines. Medics became doctors and nurses. The war had trained a generation of skilled workers.
scenes.caption: THE SKILLS CAME HOME

scenes.text: They also started businesses. Gas stations, hardware stores, car dealerships, construction companies, insurance agencies and restaurants. Many small businesses on American Main Streets in the fifties were started by veterans, often with a small loan backed by the G.I. Bill. Some of them grew into companies that still exist today.
scenes.caption: THEY STARTED BUSINESSES

scenes.text: And they brought the war's habits home with them. They were organized and disciplined. They got up early, made their beds tight, and shined their shoes. They knew how to work in teams and take orders, and how to give them. Many companies of the fifties were run like the military, by men who had learned to lead in uniform.
scenes.caption: THE HABITS CAME HOME

scenes.text: And they joined. The American Legion and the Veterans of Foreign Wars grew to millions of members. Veterans ran for city council, served on school boards and coached Little League. Many went into politics. For decades, a majority of the members of Congress were veterans. Seven men who served in the Second World War later became president.
scenes.caption: THEY JOINED

scenes.text: By nineteen fifty-five, there was a newer group of veterans too. The Korean War had begun in June of nineteen fifty and ended with a ceasefire in July of nineteen fifty-three. About one point eight million Americans served in Korea itself, and more than thirty-six thousand died there.
scenes.caption: KOREA

scenes.text: Korea was often called the forgotten war. The men who came home in fifty-three didn't get the big parades their older brothers had. The country was tired of war, and many people barely paid attention. But in towns across America, on Veterans Day of nineteen fifty-five, those younger men marched alongside the older ones.
scenes.caption: THE FORGOTTEN WAR

scenes.text: Some men had served in both wars. They had been called back from the reserves in nineteen fifty, just as they were settling down with families and jobs. For them, Korea meant leaving home a second time. They came back again, and went right back to work.
scenes.caption: THEY SERVED TWICE

scenes.text: By nineteen fifty-five, the military was also part of everyday life for young men. The draft was still in place, and most young men served two years after high school. Many were stationed in Germany, Japan or Korea, or on bases across the United States. Almost every family on the street had a son, a brother or a husband in uniform at some point.
scenes.caption: THE PEACETIME DRAFT

scenes.text: So picture that parade on November eleventh, nineteen fifty-five. At the front, a color guard carrying the flags. Then the high school band, playing a Sousa march. Then a few elderly men from the First World War, now in their sixties, riding in convertibles. And then the men from the Second World War and Korea, marching in loose rows, trying to remember how to stay in step.
scenes.caption: THE COLOR GUARD

scenes.text: Their wives watched from the sidewalk. Their children sat on their shoulders or waved little flags. Some of the kids didn't really understand what their fathers had done. They just knew Dad looked different in a uniform, and that the grown-ups around them were standing very straight and very quiet.
scenes.caption: THE CHILDREN WAVED

scenes.text: At eleven o'clock, the eleventh hour of the eleventh day, the parade stopped. A minister said a prayer. A bugler played Taps. The names of the men from town who had died were read aloud. Mothers who had lost sons stood a little apart, and other women went to stand beside them.
scenes.caption: THE ELEVENTH HOUR

scenes.text: Then the parade broke up. The men went to the American Legion hall for coffee, doughnuts and maybe something stronger. They told a few stories, but only to each other. Then they went home, had lunch, and on Monday, went back to work at the plant, the store or the office.
scenes.caption: THEN THEY WENT HOME

scenes.text: Many towns also had a war memorial in the town square, with the names of their dead carved in stone or cast in bronze. After the Second World War, new names were added beneath the names from the First World War. On Veterans Day, families laid wreaths there. Children traced the letters with their fingers, looking for their uncles and grandfathers.
scenes.caption: THE NAMES IN STONE

scenes.text: Historians and writers have called them the Greatest Generation. Most of them would have laughed at that. They didn't think of themselves as heroes. They thought they had just done their job, the same as everyone else. But what they did, both in the war and after it, shaped the country we live in.
scenes.caption: THEY DIDN'T THINK OF THEMSELVES AS HEROES

scenes.text: They raised the baby boomers. They built the suburbs, the highways and the schools. They made the American middle class. They sent their children to college in numbers no generation had ever seen. And they rarely asked for anything in return.
scenes.caption: THEY RAISED THE BABY BOOM

scenes.text: Today, almost all of them are gone. Of the sixteen million Americans who served in the Second World War, only a very small number are still alive, nearly all of them close to a hundred years old, or older. Many of their stories went untold. Their medals sit in drawers. Their letters are in shoeboxes in attics.
scenes.caption: ALMOST ALL ARE GONE

scenes.text: If your father or grandfather served, go find those letters. Look at the photographs. Ask the older members of your family what they remember. Write it down. Their stories are the story of America, and they deserve to be remembered.
scenes.caption: FIND THE LETTERS

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. Who in your family served, and where? What do you remember about them, and what did they tell you, or not tell you, about the war? We read every comment, and we would be honored to hear their names. Thank you for spending this time with me. And to every veteran watching, thank you.
scenes.caption: TELL US THEIR NAMES
